definition: A jokey “counter” to 6-7. Where 6-7 can stand in for almost anything, 41 is used as the contradictory alternative — another nonsense number kids yell back.
notes: Documented in Axis’s 2026 parent slang guide as the popular contradiction to 6-7, boosted by a rap song by Blizzi Boi that repeats “41.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A mostly meaningless Gen Alpha catchphrase (said “six-seven,” not “sixty-seven”). Kids shout it as an inside joke, a “so-so” shrug, or whenever the numbers 6 or 7 appear. The point is being in on the joke, not a secret code.
example: Teacher writes 67 on the board and the whole class yells “six-seven!”
notes: Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year. Tied to Skrilla’s song “Doot Doot (6 7),” TikToks, and NBA player LaMelo Ball (6'7"). Also written 67, 6 7, or six-seven.

definition: Coded words people use online so algorithms don’t hide the post (unalive, seggs, grape).
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: self-censored language used to bypass content moderation.

definition: Did something so well there’s nothing left to improve. Often “ate and left no crumbs.” Not about food.
example: “She sang the whole song a cappella. Ate and left no crumbs.”
notes: Axis 2026 and WeAreLuna 2026. Related to “devoured” / “served.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: The vibe or cool-factor someone gives off. Not mystical — more like “main-character energy.” Doing something impressive “gives aura.”
example: “He hit the game-winner. His aura goes crazy.”
notes: Axis 2026: “describes the vibe somebody gives off.” Related to the scoring joke “aura points.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Deliberately doing small, cool-looking things to look effortlessly impressive — posing, walking slowly off the court, posting gym pics for the vibe.
example: “Posting a silent gym selfie every morning is just aura farming.”
notes: On Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year shortlist and Oxford’s 2025 shortlist (“deliberate cultivation of an impressive public persona”).

definition: A pretend scoreboard for how cool you are. You “gain aura points” for something smooth and “lose aura points” for something awkward.
example: “He lost aura points for tripping on the way to the free-throw line.”
notes: Documented by Axis (2026) and Bark (2026). In August 2026 news, cities even used “aura points” in teen e-bike safety campaigns.

definition: A compliment: a confident, stylish, attractive woman. “Bad” here means good.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; also Axis / Wikipedia 2020s glossary.

definition: Unbothered by what other people think; speaking your mind. Can also mean “I agree with that take.”
example: “He wore the same hoodie all week. Based.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “unconcerned with what others think.”

definition: Unoriginal — into only the most mainstream things. Often teasing, not a deep insult.
example: “Pumpkin spice in September? A little basic.”
notes: Axis 2026: someone who lacks originality and likes predictable mainstream things.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Staying in bed for hours on purpose — scrolling, snacking, not being productive. Can be a cozy protest or a mental-health red flag, depending on how often it happens.
example: “Saturday is for bed rot. Do not disturb.”
notes: Axis 2026: lying in bed for hours, sometimes as a critique of hustle culture.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A quirk that isn’t good or bad — just oddly specific. Between a red flag (warning) and a green flag (good sign).
example: “His beige flag is that he sleeps in his shirts backwards.”
notes: Axis 2026. Dating-app language that kids now use about anyone’s habits.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Best friend. Used sincerely or sarcastically (“okay bestie”).
notes: Axis 2026. Everyday teen English, online and off.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A casual “okay,” “deal,” or “you bet.” Agreement, not a wager.
notes: Axis 2026 and Yahoo 2026: a shortened “you bet” used as an interjected yes.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Fancy, extra, or trying to look high-class. From “bourgeois.” Can be a compliment or a tease.
notes: Axis 2026. Also spelled boujee.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: The foggy, fried feeling after too much mindless scrolling — or the junk content itself. Teens say it jokingly about their own TikTok habits.
example: “I watched skibidi compilations for an hour. Peak brain rot.”
notes: Oxford’s 2024 Word of the Year; still listed as current in Axis and Bark’s 2026 parent guides. Also written brainrot.

definition: Bros / guy friends. Part of the -uzz family (huzz, bruzz, gruzz).
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna’s huzz explainer lists bruzz as male friends.

definition: Really, really good — almost always about food. Doubled for extra praise: “bussin’ bussin’.”
notes: Axis 2026. AAVE that went mainstream via TikTok food reviews.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A formative moment you just have to live through — awkward, hard, or lucky — as if it were written into your story.
example: “Failing the driving test is a canon event.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a formative life experience; a relatable episode of good fortune or hardship.”

definition: A lie or exaggeration. Opposite of “no cap.”
example: “He said he met her. That’s cap.”
notes: Axis 2026: Cap / No Cap = lying, or not lying.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Caught doing something wrong or embarrassing, with clear proof (as if filmed in 4K).
example: “Mom saw the grades portal. Caught in 4K.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Talking to an imaginary audience the way a livestreamer says “chat.” Kids say it out loud to nobody in particular.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang (streamer talk that left the internet).

definition: Trying too hard / outdated millennial-cool. Off-trend in a try-hard way.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: A silly fill-in phrase with no set meaning — like 6-7. From a song that just repeats “chicken, banana.” Kids use it as a joke answer to anything.
notes: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026 and Clarion Ledger (2026): a nonsense stand-in that never unseated 6-7.
sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

definition: Unattractive or undesirable — of a person or a thing. “He’s chopped” = not cute.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang, citing The New York Times (Aug 2025): “unattractive, ugly, not good looking.” Roots in African American English.

definition: a less attractive version of someone or something
notes: Copied from Merriam-Webster’s live slang dictionary on 2026-08-12 after it appeared in today's slang news.

definition: So deep in the internet that real life is the side quest. Often a tease.
notes: Common 2020s descriptor in parent and culture writing about teen internet use.
sourceName: Wikipedia — Glossary of 2020s slang (related internet slang)

definition: A mocking nickname for a clumsy or annoying AI / robot — the way someone might mutter at a chatbot that just made something up.
example: “The homework helper just invented a citation. Stupid clanker.”
notes: Macquarie Dictionary’s 2025 honourable mentions: colloquial, often derogatory, for an AI system doing human tasks poorly.

definition: Notice it / mark it / I see what you did. A “gotcha” or “write that down.”
notes: A middle-school teacher and students listed “clock it” among top-tier terms in a 2025 Scripps/NBC classroom interview, alongside 6-7 and huzz.
sourceName: NBC 26 / Scripps News classroom slang report (2025)

definition: Attention, fame, or online popularity. “Clout chasing” = doing things just to get noticed.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: In big trouble, exhausted, or done for. “I’m so cooked” = this will not end well. Different from “cooking,” which means doing well.
example: “If Mom sees this grade I’m cooked.”
notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ slang guide. Contrast with “let him cook.”
sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

definition: To snap — do something reckless or overly emotional because you’re not okay. Can mean a real spiral or just “I’m about to lose it.”
example: “My crush left me on read. I’m about to crash out.”
notes: Axis 2026: “to do something dangerous or reckless that you might regret because you aren’t feeling emotionally stable.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Secondhand-embarrassment level awkward. If something is cringey, people want to look away.
example: “Dad dancing at the barbecue is cringey.”
notes: Axis 2026: “cringe-worthy, awkward.” Also just “cringe.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Cold-weather stretch when people pair up so they are not single all winter.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Delusional — usually said jokingly about an unrealistic crush or plan. Audaciously self-confident.
example: “She thinks that celebrity liked her comment. She’s delulu.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “delusional; audaciously self-confident.”

definition: Great style — clothes, sneakers, accessories. “He has drip” means he looks put-together and fashionable.
notes: Bark 2026: “style, great fashion sense, flashy accessories.” Hip-hop fashion slang that kids still use.

definition: Agreement — “true,” “I agree.”
notes: Axis 2026.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Close friends, treated like family. A greeting as much as a noun.
notes: Bark 2026. Older hip-hop / internet slang that kids still use for their friend group.

definition: Playfully stealing a bite of someone else’s food. Named after streamer Fanum.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “taking someone else’s food; an Internet gibberish term.”

definition: Going to / about to. From “fixing to.”
notes: Axis 2026: a contraction of “fixing to.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A second, more private Instagram — “fake Insta.” Often for close friends only. Can also be used to lurk on someone quietly.
example: “I posted that on my finsta, not the real one.”
notes: Axis 2026; Bark 2026. Merriam-Webster has also entered the word.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Amazing or excellent. Also the 🔥 emoji.
notes: Bark 2026 and Axis 2026 parent guides.

definition: Showing off an outfit (or several) — usually a quick video or photo dump. “Fit” = outfit.
notes: WeAreLuna 2026: showing off your outfit, often as a social-video trend.

definition: To show off. Can be a verb (“stop flexing”) or a noun (“that’s a flex”). Not always an insult — sometimes just bragging rights.
example: “Not to flex, but we have early dismissal.”
notes: WeAreLuna and Gabb 2026 parent guides. Older gym slang (“flex your muscles”) applied to anything brag-worthy.

definition: A stretch when nothing is working — looks, posts, or life. Temporary, usually joked about.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna 2026 also lists it.

definition: Fear of missing out.
notes: Bark 2026.

definition: “For real.” Agreement or emphasis. “BFFR” / “be so FR” = “be serious.”
notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Axis also lists BFFR / BFR / Be So FR as expressions of disbelief.

definition: A blank, deadpan look younger workers or teens give when a request feels obvious, awkward, or “boomer.” Not always rude on purpose — sometimes it’s just the face.
example: “I asked if they could work Saturday and got the Gen Z stare.”
notes: On Dictionary.com’s 2025 Word of the Year shortlist. A workplace/culture meme about generational deadpan.

definition: Suddenly ignoring someone — no texts, no explanation.
notes: Common in 2026 parent slang lists (Bark, Game Quitters, Shorelight).

definition: A snacky, uncooked “meal” of whatever is in the fridge — cheese, crackers, leftover fries — instead of a plated dinner.
example: “Girl dinner is pickles and a string cheese.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a light meal of snacks or easy-to-prepare foods.”

definition: A joking way to justify spending — “I returned something, so this purchase is free.” An inside joke; sometimes used to mock women and money.
example: “I returned the shoes, so this concert is girl math free.”
notes: Axis 2026 parent guide; We Are Teachers 2026 slang list.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: To over-praise someone in a way that feels fake or excessive. If a friend is “glazing” a celebrity, they’re laying it on too thick.
example: “Stop glazing him — he missed half his shots.”
notes: Merriam-Webster and Cambridge’s 2025 watchlists; Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide. Also “glazing.”
sourceName: Merriam-Webster; Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

definition: A big improvement in looks, style, or life. “She had a glow-up over the summer.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Greatest of all time. A huge compliment.
notes: Merriam-Webster added GOAT / goated; still everyday teen praise.

definition: A good sign in a person — the opposite of a red flag.
example: “He thanked the bus driver. Green flag.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; dating-app language kids now use about anyone.

definition: The opposite of low-key: obviously, seriously, not hiding it.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “straight up, seriously, extremely.”

definition: Hits in a uniquely stronger or more emotional way than usual.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Hit me up — text me / get in touch.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Take the loss. Admit you were wrong or you lost.
example: “You missed the shot. Hold the L.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to admit being wrong or to accept defeat.” L = loss.

definition: Internet slang for girls / women. Some kids use it like “crush.” It comes from a mangled, disrespectful word for women (hoes), so it is not polite even when they mean it playfully.
example: “I tripped in front of the huzz.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “online slang for ‘women.’” WeAreLuna and NBC classroom reports cover the teen use.

definition: Excitement around something — or the act of pumping someone up. “I finally get the hype” = I see why people like this.
example: “I finally get the hype around that show.”
notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Everyday sports/marketing English that teens use as a noun and verb.

definition: A sudden feeling of disgust or repulsion, often about a crush’s small habit.
example: “He chews with his mouth open. Instant ick.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a feeling of disgust or repulsion.”

definition: I just burst out laughing. A newer stand-in for LOL.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Used to name a vibe or look: “It’s giving 2000s movie star.”
example: “That jacket? It’s giving coach on the sideline.”
notes: Ballroom / internet slang listed across 2026 parent and social-media slang guides.

definition: “If you know, you know.” An inside joke — if you get it, you’re in the group.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: A loss. “Take the L” = accept you lost.
notes: Axis 2026.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Let someone keep going — they’re on a roll. “Cooking” = performing well. Don’t interrupt; they’re about to do something good.
example: “Don’t cut him off, let him cook.”
notes: Yahoo 2026 parent guide; common sports and streamer slang. Opposite vibe of “cooked.”
sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

definition: To enter a state of deep focus. “I’m locked in” = I’m concentrating, don’t interrupt.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to enter a state of deep focus.”

definition: Going all-in on looking more attractive — skincare, gym, sometimes extreme or unsafe advice from online forums.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: efforts, sometimes extreme, young men take to look more attractive.

definition: A little / secretly / not making a big deal of it. Opposite of high-key.
notes: Merriam-Webster / everyday teen English; Axis and parent guides list it as current.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A mashed-up intensifier: “low-key” + “genuinely.” Used like “literally” or “honestly.” Brain-rot word-building, not a secret meaning.
example: “The store is lowkenuinely out of iced tea.”
notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide, citing The New York Times: a brain-rot blend used in place of “literally,” “low-key,” or “genuinely.”

definition: Acting like the star of the movie — confident, a little dramatic, center of the story.
example: “Walking into school with coffee and headphones. Main character energy.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “dramatic self-confidence; obtrusive self-importance.”

definition: Korean 말랑 / 말랑말랑 (mallang, mallangmallang) means soft, squishy, or fluffy. That is where the character name Molang comes from. It is a real Korean word for texture, not a teen code language.
example: A Korean speaker might call a mochi “mallangmallang” — soft and squishy.
notes: Hye-Ji Yoon has said Molang’s name comes from “mallang~ mallang.” Some fan wikis also note 몰라 (molla, “I don’t know”) as a look-alike, but the designer’s stated source is mallang = soft.
sourceName: Korean mallang / mallangmallang; Molang name origin (Hye-Ji Yoon)

definition: A tongue-posture trend claimed (without solid medical proof) to sharpen the jawline. Kids may sit in class pressing their tongue to the roof of the mouth.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a tongue technique purported to enhance one’s jaw and face.”

definition: Of mediocre or disappointing quality. Not terrible — just nothing special.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Visibly outshining someone — looking better, playing better, taking the spotlight. “He’s mogging me in this photo” = he looks way better.
example: “Don’t stand next to him in group pics, he’ll mog you.”
notes: From AMOG, “alpha male of the group” (noted by Psychology Today). Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide covers the current teen use.
sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026

definition: The round white bunny from the kids’ show Molang. Not a secret code. The name comes from Korean 말랑말랑 (mallangmallang) — “soft, squishy, fluffy.” Kids say it like a character name, or for something cute and squishy.
notes: Created by Korean illustrator Hye-Ji Yoon (2010), animated by France’s Millimages. Designer said the name is from mallang / mallangmallang. The characters do not speak English — they use a made-up sound language called Molanguese.

definition: The show’s made-up “language”: cute babbles and sound effects, not real words. Millimages created it so kids anywhere can follow the feelings without translation. If your child is “speaking Molang,” they are mimicking those noises — there is no hidden vocabulary to decode.
example: Molang and Piu Piu only “talk” in Molanguese on the show.
notes: Millimages (official): Molanguese was created so anyone, anywhere, could understand Molang emotionally without needing words. Also called Molangish in some fan write-ups. The series is produced as non-dialogue.

definition: “No lie” / “I’m serious.” “Cap” means a lie or exaggeration; “no cap” means this is the truth.
example: “I didn’t study and still got an A, no cap.”
notes: Axis 2026: “Cap/No Cap = Lying, or not lying.” Long-running hip-hop slang that teens still use daily.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Someone acting robotic or on autopilot, like a video-game extra with no free will. Often a tease, sometimes unkind.
example: “He just repeats whatever the group says. NPC behavior.”
notes: From “non-player character” in games. Common in 2020s youth slang glossaries.

definition: Weird, awkward, cringeworthy, or just bad — not the state. “That’s so Ohio” = that’s bizarre. From “only in Ohio” memes that treated Ohio as a place where surreal things happen.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “weird, awkward, cringeworthy.” Also covered in parent explainers (Screenwise, Tinybeans).

definition: A brush-off for an older person (or anyone sounding old) who doesn’t get it.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; Axis 2026 still lists it.

definition: Acting wild, inappropriate, or way out of line.
example: “Yelling at the ref like that was out of pocket.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: A one-sided “relationship” a fan feels with a celebrity, influencer, or even an AI chatbot. The famous person does not know the fan; the fan still feels close.
example: “She has a parasocial thing with that podcast host — she talks like they’re friends.”
notes: Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2025. An older psychology term that went mainstream as influencer culture and AI companions grew.
sourceName: Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2025

definition: The person who rides shotgun and does not drive — usually treated like royalty.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: End of discussion. A louder “period.”
notes: Common in 2026 Gen Alpha slang lists (Hoomale and others).

definition: Two different things: (1) Molang’s chick friend is named Piu Piu — kids say it like “pew pew.” (2) As slang/algospeak, “pew pew” is the laser/gun sound; Wiktionary also lists it as a firearm. Ask which one they mean.
example: “He went pew pew in the game.” / (online) “No pew pews in the backpack.”
notes: Wiktionary lists pew pew as a noun meaning a firearm. Parents and teachers also flag it as a censorship workaround for “gun.”

definition: Someone who puts other people down to look more likable — “I’m not like other girls/guys.”
example: “She called all the other girls basic. Pick-me behavior.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Molang’s best friend: a small yellow chick. Shy, careful, the voice of reason. Kids often say the name like “pew pew.” Not a gun joke in this context — it’s the character.
example: “I want the Piu Piu plush, not just Molang.”
notes: Official Molang franchise (Millimages / shop.molang.com): Molang and best friend chick Piu Piu.

definition: A cutesy pet name for someone you love — a partner, a best friend, even a parent.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a term of endearment.” In print since the mid-1960s; kids still use it.

definition: Online content made to make you angry so you comment, share, and keep the algorithm fed. If a post seems designed to wind people up, it is probably rage bait.
example: “Don’t reply — that headline is pure rage bait.”
notes: Oxford University Press Word of the Year 2025, after recorded usage roughly tripled. Cousin of “clickbait,” but the hook is outrage, not curiosity.
sourceName: Oxford University Press Word of the Year 2025

definition: When a reply gets more likes than the original post — usually meaning the original take flopped.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang / common social-media English.

definition: A warning sign — something that makes you think twice about a person or situation.
example: “He got mad that I had other friends. Red flag.”
notes: Long-running dating slang; still listed in current parent slang guides.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Stuck in your head. If something “lives rent-free” in your mind, you can’t stop thinking about it.
example: “That song is living rent-free in my head.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: preoccupied with someone or something.

definition: Short for charisma: someone’s ability to charm or flirt. “W rizz” = good game; “L rizz” or “negative rizz” = striking out.
example: “He actually got her number? W rizz.”
notes: From “charisma.” Oxford’s 2023 Word of the Year; still in everyday teen use and defined on Wiktionary as the ability to attract a love interest.

definition: Bitter, annoyed, or sore about something — usually a small slight.
example: “He’s still salty he didn’t get picked.”
notes: Bark 2026: “to be bitter or cranky about something.” Long-running, still current.

definition: A drawn-out “wow” — surprise, impress, or “that’s a lot.” Often with a hand gesture.
notes: Listed in 2026 Gen Alpha parent slang roundups as an expression of surprise or disbelief.

definition: A skeptical or judging glance — or talking about that glance. “Side eye” in a text means “I’m judging this.”
example: “She said she ‘forgot’ her homework… side eye.”
notes: WeAreLuna 2026 and Slang.net’s daily slang (August 2026: “a disapproving glance”).

definition: A detour from the main plan — like a video-game extra mission. “Stopping for snacks is a side quest.”
example: “Homework is the main quest. This show is a side quest.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: Shorthand for a lone-wolf, self-assured type — “main character” independence. Often used half-jokingly (“sigma rizz”).
example: “He skipped the party to finish his project. Sigma behavior.”
notes: From internet “sigma male” personality charts. WeAreLuna 2026: independent, confident energy. Take the meme with a grain of salt.

definition: Someone who fawns too hard — usually over a crush — and looks a little desperate doing it.
example: “He bought her lunch every day. Don’t simp.”
notes: Merriam-Webster: to show excessive devotion to someone.

definition: A romantic thing that isn’t officially a relationship — more than friends, less than dating.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; also Shorelight’s 2026 American slang list.

definition: A nonsense meme word. It can mean “bad,” “cool,” or nothing at all — mostly a silly sound kids attach to other words (“skibidi toilet,” “skibidi rizz”).
notes: From the viral YouTube/TikTok series Skibidi Toilet. Wiktionary: “a nonsense word, sometimes used to form noun adjuncts for humorous effect.”

definition: Really good — especially a song, but also food or a moment. “This slaps” = this goes hard.
example: “Have you heard the new track? It slaps.”
notes: Gabb’s 2026 parent slang list. Related to “bussin’” (usually food) and “fires.”

definition: To do something extremely well. A compliment for a look, a performance, or a comeback.
notes: Ballroom / drag culture that went fully mainstream. Listed in WeAreLuna and Gabb’s 2026 parent slang guides.

definition: To underestimate or ignore something good. “Don’t sleep on that album.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to underestimate, overlook, or ignore.”

definition: Low-quality digital junk produced in bulk, usually by AI — fake-looking videos, cheesy ads, junk e-books, almost-real fake news. People use it the way we once used “spam.”
example: “My feed is all talking-cat slop today.”
notes: Merriam-Webster’s 2025 Word of the Year. Editors chose it because lookups spiked as AI-generated content flooded social feeds.

definition: Tiny and cute. Internet spelling of small.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang; WeAreLuna 2026.

definition: Looking extremely good — outfit, makeup, or waistline. A strong compliment.
notes: WeAreLuna 2026. From drag / beauty slang; teens use it for clothes and looks.

definition: How much people-energy someone has left. When the battery is dead, they want to go home — not because they dislike you.
example: “My social battery is at 2%. I’m heading out.”
notes: WeAreLuna 2026. Introvert-internet language that teens now say out loud.

definition: A superfan — or the act of being one. “I stan her” = I’m a devoted fan. Can be affectionate or a little obsessive.
example: “I stan that author. I’ve read everything.”
notes: From Eminem’s song “Stan.” Axis 2026 still lists it as current teen vocabulary.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Backing up what you said — no empty talk. Holding a boundary or following through.
example: “She said she wouldn’t go if he was there, and she didn’t. Standing on business.”
notes: Axis 2026: “to double-down on something or stay strong in your conviction.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Short for suspicious or shady. Something (or someone) doesn’t add up.
notes: Older slang that exploded with Among Us (2018–20). Still in Axis’s 2026 dictionary.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: To be honest.
notes: Axis 2026.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Gossip. “Spill the tea” = tell me the story.
notes: Axis 2026.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: A blunt way to say “log off and go outside.” Used when someone is too online, too deep in an argument, or losing perspective.
example: “You’ve been in the comments for three hours. Touch grass.”
notes: Among Merriam-Webster’s most-looked-up words of 2025. An internet scold that became everyday slang.

definition: Cool or awesome. A respelling of “tough,” not an insult.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “cool, awesome, etc.”

definition: A coded way to say kill or die — used so social apps don’t flag the post. If a child uses this about themselves, treat it as a real safety signal, not a joke.
example: “The movie unalived the villain in the first scene.”
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a euphemism for ‘kill’ or ‘die.’” Algospeak.

definition: Short for “uncle.” A teasing name for an older person (or anyone acting old / out of touch). If your kid calls you unc, they’re saying you’re not with it.
notes: Bark’s 2026 teen-slang guide: an older, usually male figure, or anyone out of touch with current trends.

definition: Nailed it — did exactly what the moment called for, and then some.
example: “Look at that costume. She understood the assignment.”
notes: Axis 2026; We Are Teachers 2026.
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: Fair / I get it / that checks out.
notes: Everyday Gen Z English listed across 2026 slang roundups.

definition: A quick, informal read of someone’s mood or a room’s energy.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “a casual or intuitive assessment of the quality of something or someone.”

definition: A win. “That’s a W.” Opposite of L (a loss).
notes: Axis 2026: antonym of take the L; pronounced “dub.”
sourceName: Axis — A Parent’s Guide to Teen Slang (2026)

definition: October–December as a “lock-in” for goals — gym, grades, habits — before the new year. Also called the Great Lock In.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: a three-month period dedicated to focusing on goals before the new year.

definition: A trombone-style “too bad” sound, used to mock a small failure.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: used to mock someone else’s misfortune or disappointment.

definition: “What you look like?” A request for a photo. Bark flags this: strangers on apps often lead with WYLL — kids should be careful before sending pictures.
example: “I matched with someone and the first message was WYLL.”
notes: Bark 2026 teen text-codes guide.

definition: Someone who talks a lot. “Yapping” = chatting nonstop. Usually affectionate, sometimes “please stop.”
example: “Sorry, I’m such a yapper when I’m nervous.”
notes: WeAreLuna 2026 lists yapper / yap / yapping. Related joke: “yappuccino.”

definition: To pile beauty filters on a photo until it looks ultra-glam and a little fake.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang: “to heavily edit an image with beauty filters.” WeAreLuna 2026 also lists it.

definition: You only live once — used to justify a risky or fun choice.
notes: Merriam-Webster Slang.

definition: A hype phrase: you are the guy. The main character. The one everyone wants to be in this moment. Works for any gender in practice.
example: “You cooked dinner and fixed the Wi-Fi? You’re him.”
notes: Yahoo’s 2026 parents’ guide: hyping someone as the person everyone wants to be.
sourceName: Yahoo Parents’ Guide to Teen Slang 2026
